chapter: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
title: Music as therapy and Rachmaninoff after his chest surgery
summary: Willard and Jones discuss music as therapy and his hospital recovery with Rachmaninoff and Ravel records.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah, I think music is therapy for a lot of people.

Yeah. But no matter what else is going on. Oh, this might refer to the question you asked me before, have you ever tried to analyze why, under certain circumstances, when things are in a negative state, that you still play well or even better. I just think the music is built in, and it's like -- I believe you said the right thing, it's therapy.
I think so sometimes. I know Louis Bellson's talked about this a lot.

He feels that music is the answer to every kind of disturbance. It would level off the world, emotional disturbances of every kind. And he studied. He's done research on some of the times that music has helped in hospitals, with physical therapy and with emotional and mental therapy.

Yeah. I was getting ready to bring that up. When I had surgery, chest surgery, some years back, after they brought me down from the operating room and to go -- there was just two patients in a room -- they would bring music in. Not pain killers. And with me it worked. I would just doze off to sleep, and soon I slept myself back to health. But it was experimental at that point. I'm going back to 1951, '52. But it worked very well. And music was the -- I'll never forget what I asked for. It was Rachmaninoff.
And they asked you what you would like to hear?
Gave you a choice. Rachmaninoff and Ravel. Because if I had listened to Ellington at that point I'd have been a nervous wreck.
You have to be on your toes to listen to Duke.
